title: Arlo's Speedy Sled Surprise
markdown:
The sky cracked open like a golden egg and spilled sunshine. Sunbeams, warm as spilled honey, splashed across Arlo’s workshop. He stretched, a rumbling yawn. “Epic parcel day.” A super-important package for Auntie Noor, tied with a ribbon the colour of summer sky, needed to get there fast.

He had built a parcel sled: bouncy springs that could leap a puddle, gears that whirred with precision, a little flag that served no purpose except joy. “Zoom!” A happy vigorous push. It glided from the doorstep and picked up speed on the smooth paved road, ribbon fluttering as if it already knew Auntie Noor’s gate. “Spectacular.” Then the path turned. A newly laid grassy track, still sparkling with dew, laid by someone who had not asked a sled its opinion. The sled bucked. Jolt. It stopped dead — THUMP — and a rough grating GRIND spoiled the morning. The package tipped, then settled, still tied, which was the only mercy.

Tansy the squirrel, tail a bushy question mark, popped from behind a sturdy acorn. “Trouble, Arlo? Big trouble?” Nose twitching, she darted closer.

Arlo sighed, cheeks puffing. He wiped grease from his brow. “This grass is grabby. It’s hugging the sled.” He shoved with all his strength. A slow agonizing drag, then stubborn stop. “Like thick mud after rain.”

Tansy scampered the grassy path, tiny paws barely touching, then flicked onto the packed-earth trail beside it. Back and forth, a brown blur. “This bit is speedy!” Then the grass again. “This bit is PUSH-y. It fights back!”

Arlo watched. On the tufts her paws gripped and dug. On the packed earth her feet barely sounded. His sled wheels were round and bouncy, made for smooth travel; on the yielding grass they sank a little. He touched the blades — ticklish, rough. The packed earth beside: smooth, almost slick, like well-worn stone.

“Grabby and fighting back.” A flicker. He looked at the solid hard-wood wheels. “What if we made them less grabby?”

Tansy tilted her head. “Less grabby?”

He rubbed a small smooth stone against one wheel. “The stone slides. Doesn’t catch. The grass catches the wheels. Sandpaper versus ice.”

“Ice is super slippy!” She bounced.

He remembered Auntie Noor’s pantry: polished jars, waxy apples like silk. He dashed to the workshop, rummaged, found smooth polished planks and thick waxy leaves. He shaped small discs of the polished wood and fixed them to the sides of the wheels, little shields meant to glide.

“Best seat in the house.” He pushed the sled onto the grass. The discs spun, smooth surfaces barely catching. No jolt. No grind. It glided, silent and swift.

“WHOOSH!” Tansy leapt onto the back as it sailed past. They reached Noor’s cottage as the sun hit its peak. The parcel arrived with the ribbon still tidy.

Noor beamed. “A wonderfully speedy delivery. How did you manage that grassy path?”

Arlo patted the sled. “Tansy’s eyes and legs. The grass rubbed and slowed us. We made the wheels smoother, and they zipped.” He used the word once, without a muscle-power closer: friction.

Tansy flicked her tail. “Push-y became speedy.”

Noor chuckled and did not wink them into a speech. She cut the pie because the parcel was on time, which was reason enough. Arlo and Tansy took slices and did not announce that the day was just beginning. The sled, cooling by the step, had already made its point.
